descripcion: At C2 idioms are deployed and consciously twisted for effect — modifying a fixed idiom slightly for humour or precision, and recognising when a native speaker's own twist on an idiom is play rather than an error, which is the mark of full idiomatic command.

filas: to go round in ever-smaller circles
to cut a long story short
to cut an already short story shorter

ejemplos.texto: We're not just going round in circles — we're going round in ever-smaller ones.
It was less a storm in a teacup and more a hurricane in one.
To cut an already short story shorter, it didn't work.

notas: Twisting a fixed idiom deliberately signals full command of the original — it only works if the standard form is obviously the base being played with.
This kind of play belongs in informal or witty registers; using it in a formal document undermines the intended effect.
A twist should still be recognisable as the source idiom — too much distortion just reads as a mistake.

es.en: Spanish speakers know idioms well, but may take a deliberately modified English idiom as a native speaker's mistake. Recognising the twist as intentional requires knowing the original English form.
es.es: Los hispanohablantes conocen bien los modismos, pero pueden interpretar un modismo inglés modificado deliberadamente como un error de un nativo. Reconocer que el giro es intencionado exige conocer la forma inglesa original.

de.en: German headlines also twist idioms for effect, so the technique is familiar. The difficulty is recognising the English base idiom behind the twist.
de.de: Auch deutsche Schlagzeilen spielen mit Redewendungen, daher ist die Technik vertraut. Die Schwierigkeit liegt darin, die englische Grundredensart hinter der Abwandlung zu erkennen.

it.en: Italian headlines and advertising also twist idioms, so the technique is familiar. The difficulty is recognising the English base idiom behind the twist.
it.it: Anche titoli e pubblicità italiani modificano idiomi per creare effetto, quindi la tecnica è familiare. La difficoltà sta nel riconoscere l'idiom inglese di base dietro la variazione.

fr.en: French headlines play constantly with fixed expressions, so the technique is very familiar. The difficulty is recognising the English base idiom behind the twist.
fr.fr: Les titres français jouent constamment avec les expressions figées, donc la technique est très familière. La difficulté consiste à reconnaître l'idiome anglais de base derrière la variation.

pt.en: Portuguese headlines and advertising also twist idioms, so the technique is familiar. The difficulty is recognising the English base idiom behind the twist.
pt.pt: Manchetes e publicidade em português também brincam com idioms, então a técnica é familiar. A dificuldade está em reconhecer o idiom inglês original por trás da alteração.

errores: Twisting an idiom the speaker doesn't actually know the standard form of, which reads as an error rather than play.
Using idiom play in a register where it undermines credibility.
Distorting the idiom so far that the source is no longer recognisable.

autochequeo: Is the source idiom being twisted still clearly recognisable?
Does the register fit deliberate idiom play, not formal writing?
Would a native reader read this as play, not as an error?
Is the twist used sparingly, for a specific effect?
Do I know the standard form of every idiom I'm twisting?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on deliberate idiom twists. Check whether the source idiom remains recognisable and whether the register fits. Do not rewrite the text. Flag anything that reads as an error rather than deliberate play.

es: «*No hay mal que por bien no venga*» rendered as *There's no bad that doesn't come for good* instead of *Every cloud has a silver lining*.
de: *Jetzt haben wir den Salat* rendered as *Now we have the salad* instead of *Now we're in a mess*.
it: «*Non tutto il male vien per nuocere*» rendered as *Not all evil comes to harm* instead of *Every cloud has a silver lining*.
fr: «*À quelque chose malheur est bon*» rendered as *To something misfortune is good* instead of *Every cloud has a silver lining*.
pt: «*Há males que vêm por bem*» rendered as *There are evils that come for good* instead of *Every cloud has a silver lining*.
